item.title: FBI warns ongoing FortiBleed attacks lock out legitimate FortiGate firewall and SSL VPN administrators
item.description:
Federal law enforcement authorities have issued an urgent cyber alert warning of widespread ongoing exploitation targeting perimeter firewall infrastructure. Threat actors leverage memory corruption flaws to steal active administrative cookies and lock enterprise security teams out of management dashboards.
The threat campaign, dubbed FortiBleed, targets exposed Fortinet FortiGate firewalls and SSL VPN gateways across enterprise networks. Threat actors transmit malformed authentication requests to extract cleartext administrative session tokens and credentials from system memory. Upon gaining access, adversaries revoke legitimate administrative accounts, reconfigure local firewall rules, and establish persistent SSL VPN backdoors across perimeter gateways. FBI advisories urge immediate session termination and out-of-band credential resets.
Subverting perimeter firewall management controls destroys enterprise network isolation. Because FortiGate gateways manage perimeter access policies and site-to-site VPN tunnels, an administrative lockout permits threat actors to manipulate traffic routing rules, disable security inspection daemons, and pivot into internal subnets.
- Execute out-of-band administrative credential resets across all managed Fortinet FortiGate appliances immediately. - Invalidate all active SSL VPN and web administration session tokens across firewalls using console CLI access. - Restrict public internet access to FortiGate management interfaces by placing admin panels on dedicated out-of-band management VLANs. - Inspect system access logs and administrator registries for unauthorized user creations or altered account permissions.
Perimeter firewall defense demands strict control plane isolation and rapid session revoking protocols to ensure network security controllers remain protected from unauthenticated session hijacking. #CodeDefence #Fortinet #FortiGate #FortiBleed #SSLVPN #Firewall #CISA #IncidentResponse #AppSec

item.title: PoeLLM malware chains AI server vulnerabilities CVE-2026-42271 and CVE-2026-48710 in cryptomining campaigns
item.description:
Threat research disclosures published today reveal a novel malware family abusing artificial intelligence server infrastructure. Threat actors chain Model Context Protocol test endpoint flaws with authentication bypasses to execute arbitrary system code and deploy persistent mining payloads.
The malware campaign, dubbed PoeLLM, targets exposed LiteLLM and Gotenberg AI servers. Adversaries chain LiteLLM MCP test endpoint vulnerability CVE-2026-42271 with unauthenticated access flaw CVE-2026-48710 to achieve remote code execution. PoeLLM utilizes a unique command and control C2 mechanism that translates poetic text blocks into IP addresses, deploying XMRig miners and reverse shell scripts across compromised AI build nodes. Threat telemetry confirms compromised servers actively scan internal subnets on ports 3000 and 4000.
Subverting artificial intelligence model serving nodes introduces compute hijacking and software supply chain risks. Because AI servers maintain high-performance GPU resources and API integration tokens, an unauthenticated host compromise permits threat actors to exhaust compute resources and harvest model integration keys.
- Apply official security patches published by LiteLLM maintainers across all AI server deployments immediately. - Restrict public network visibility of LiteLLM test endpoints and Model Context Protocol ports using zero trust proxies. - Inspect AI host process trees for unauthorized XMRig execution routines or anomalous port scanning activity. - Rotate all API integration tokens and model repository credentials processed on exposed AI application servers.
AI infrastructure defense relies on strict endpoint authentication and continuous process monitoring to ensure machine learning build nodes remain protected against unauthenticated exploit chains. #CodeDefence #LiteLLM #AISecurity #PoeLLM #RCE #CryptoMining #AppSec #DevSecOps #PatchManagement

item.title: Threat actors hijack ccTLD registries to obtain unauthorized Let us Encrypt SSL certificates for Google domains
item.description:
Cyber threat investigation writeups published today detail a major domain name system registry breach impacting global web traffic. Threat actors subverted authoritative regional top-level domain registries to request valid SSL TLS certificates for major technology platforms.
The infrastructure breach targeted country-code top-level domain ccTLD registries for Ghana .gh, American Samoa .as, and Sierra Leone .sl. Threat actors modified authoritative DNS records to pass domain validation checks, generating 12 valid Let us Encrypt and ZeroSSL certificates for regional Google and YouTube domains. The attack allowed adversaries to conduct man-in-the-middle decryption of user web traffic until Certificate Transparency log monitoring enabled Google to revoke affected certificates and block them in Chrome.
Subverting domain registry infrastructure undermines global public key infrastructure trust boundaries. When threat actors compromise authoritative ccTLD operators, adversaries can generate valid SSL certificates for target domains, enabling stealthy traffic interception without triggering browser security warnings.
- Publish strict Certification Authority Authorization CAA records across all corporate domain portfolios to restrict certificate issuance. - Implement real-time Certificate Transparency CT log monitoring to detect unauthorized certificate requests across regional domain assets. - Restrict internal administrative access to corporate domain registrar portals using hardware-based multi-factor authentication. - Report unverified certificate issuances immediately to issuing Certificate Authorities to force rapid revocation protocols.
Domain infrastructure security demands rigorous CAA record enforcement and continuous Certificate Transparency monitoring to ensure corporate web domains remain protected against registry hijacking. #CodeDefence #Google #DNS #PKI #CertificateTransparency #DomainSecurity #WebSecurity #AppSec
